etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English newes, newys (“new things”), equivalent to new (noun) +‎ -s. Compare Saterland Frisian Näis (“news”), East Frisian näjs (“news”), West Frisian nijs (“news”), Dutch nieuws (“news”), German Low German Neeis (“new things; news”), though unlike the English word, these originated as genitives, not plurals. Sometimes erroneously claimed to be an acronym of "North, East, West, South" or "Noteworthy Events, Weather, Sports".

quote.citation: 1593, anonymous author, The Life and Death of Iacke Straw […], Act I:
quote.text: VVith speede let vs impart the newes vnto my Lord the King,The fearefull newes that whilſt the flame doth but begin,Sad pollicie may ſerue to quench the fire:  […]

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii], page 239, column 1:
quote.text: Sirra, your Lord and maſters married, there's newes for you: you haue a new Miſtris.

quote.citation: a. 1630, David Hume of Godscroft, The History of the Houses of Douglas and Angus, Edinburgh:  […]  Evan Tyler, […], published 1644, page 302:
quote.text: When theſe news were brought to him, ſome counſelled him to go to Stirlin, where the King was, and where he would be the ſtronger.

definitions.definition: Information about current events disseminated by the media.

quote.citation: 2012, Christopher Lueg, Danyel Fisher, From Usenet to CoWebs, page 207:
quote.text: The Usenet news system brings people together from around the world and forms social groups on the basis of common interest. Usenet news is a domain that is suffering badly from information overload.

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To report; to make known.

quote.text: This remark was newsed abroad; whereupon the loyal authorities of Lerwick immediately had the revolutionary skipper arrested, on a charge of high treason.
